doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: German occupation of Denmark and escape to Sweden; father's flight via Varian Fry
summary: He recalls the Nazi arrival in Vienna and Copenhagen, the 1943 rescue of Danish Jews to Sweden, and his father's escape through France and Lisbon to the US.

blocks.x: And you yourself had a — I guess after going to Denmark there was an underground system?

Yeah. Well actually, this is April 9th is not? It is April 9th today? April 9th was the day that the Germans occupied Denmark. April 9, 1940. I remember it very well because it was the second time in my life that Nazis marched into a city that I was living in. When I was in Vienna I had scarlet fever at the time of the Anschluss. But I remember, that was considered a serious illness then, and that was one reason why my mother stayed with me and my father had to get out in a hurry. So he split and went to France. That’s a whole other story. But I remember the yelling and screaming. The Viennese, they would like to forget about that now, but the majority welcomed Hitler. And I remember that noise from everybody screaming “Heil.” And then on April 9th, 1940 I was asleep. My bedroom had sort of a slanted window. We were living on the top floor of a building in Copenhagen and there was like one room that had this — it was almost like a — it would have been a © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

good place for a painter, for a studio, because there was plenty of light. And when I woke up I heard planes and I looked out and I could see the German — that cross that they had on their wings there, and then the swastika on the tail. So that was the Germans coming into Denmark, which was not a happy awakening. The planes dropped leaflets that the Germans had come to protect Denmark against the British and whatever. Anyway, it was interesting because the early part of the occupation, the Germans needed Denmark as a larder. Denmark was a major producer and exporter of foods — dairy products and pork especially, bacon and eggs, butter, milk and everything. And the Germans could use all that stuff. So they called Denmark, they called it, that was like their window to the world that they could behave themselves, which they did for a while. But in spite of that there were all kinds of things that happened which the Danes did not relish and the underground developed gradually and also the Germans started behaving differently. But in 1943, in the fall of 1943, they decided to round up all the Jews in Denmark. It wasn’t a very large population but the underground was prepared for that, and they had managed to obtain the list that the Germans had of who they were going to arrest. And so, I mean I don’t really want to get — I want to talk about jazz I guess, but what happened was at 4 o’clock in the afternoon one day, it was in September I guess, or early October, before my birthday, knocked on the door, opened the door and there was this nice young man who said, “May I come in I have something important to talk to you about.” And he gave my mother and I instructions, detailed instructions, about what to do, where to go, don’t pack anything except maybe an overnight thing, don’t tell anybody, we will inform people, don’t worry about what’s in your apartment, just get out and meet at a certain place. And then we met there with other people and they gave us some money for travel and told us what tickets to get on a train — the whole thing was very well organized. As it happened the first attempt did fail and then there was about a period of almost a week when I was planted at different people’s homes overnight and stuff, and then we got out to Sweden, which there’s this narrow body of water between Denmark and Sweden. And the Swedes, who were neutral, accepted both Norwegian and Danish — Norway was also occupied by Germans — refugees. And so I came to Sweden in October of ’43 and spent a year and a half until the war ended in Sweden, and then went back to Denmark. And my father in the meantime had adventures in France where he was interned by the French and eventually the French turned that internment camp over to the Germans, but he managed to get away and made his way to Vichy, was in Marseilles, was assisted by this great American named — what was his name — Varian Fry — he was a civilian. He didn’t have any — the State Department was very ambiguous about helping Jewish refugees, it was limited what they would accept. But he went to Marseilles and he managed to get a lot of people out, including my father. He got my father a Honduran passport, which was © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

something that you could buy. He went to Morocco, and from Morocco to Lisbon. And he had long ago applied for an American visa because of all the things that happened. But once he got to Portugal he was able to get a, you know, entry, a permit to the United States and got out in April of ’41. And that was before Pearl Harbor, so we were still, we were in Denmark. In all the time that he was roaming around in France and Morocco and so on it was not — it would not have been a good idea for him to write to us because the Germans censored all the mail that came from overseas from other countries. But once he arrived here he was able to communicate with us and we knew that he was okay.
